question: In the films, the Hogwarts Express steams across a dramatic curving viaduct through the mountains, and every summer you can ride that same line on a real steam train. In which country is it?
source_excerpt: The train covers the 84-mile round trip between Fort William and Mallaig, crossing the spectacular Glenfinnan Viaduct.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the Hogwarts Express as pure movie magic or a studio set. In fact it's a real line that anyone can ride behind a steam engine, and the viaduct that looks like ancient stone is actually one of the earliest big concrete bridges.

topicality.rationale: Evergreen film/travel trivia about the Glenfinnan Viaduct and Jacobite steam train; not tied to any news event.

extra.verification_notes: Glenfinnan Viaduct, used as the Hogwarts Express route in the films, is in Scotland and the Jacobite steam train still runs over it in 2026.

explanation: It's the Glenfinnan Viaduct in the Scottish Highlands, on the Jacobite steam train route from Fort William to Mallaig. Despite its old-stone look, the viaduct is made of concrete and was built in the 1890s.

question: The Sword of Gryffindor is one of the few weapons that can destroy a Horcrux, but it didn't start out that way. What did the blade soak up in the Chamber of Secrets that gave it this power?
source_excerpt: it became infused with Basilisk venom, which made it capable of destroying Horcruxes

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the sword destroys Horcruxes because it is legendary or magical. The real reason is that it absorbed the poison of the monster Harry slew years earlier, a callback that links book 2 to book 7.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter book lore from 1998, not tied to any current news.

extra.verification_notes: Canon (Deathly Hallows) says the sword absorbed basilisk venom when Harry killed the Basilisk in the Chamber, giving it Horcrux-destroying power; I found no newer development that changes this.

explanation: Goblin-made blades absorb whatever makes them stronger. When Harry drove the sword into the basilisk, it took in the venom, which made it a Horcrux-killer for the rest of the saga.

question: Dumbledore's blackened, cursed hand came from putting on a Horcrux ring he knew was dangerous. Its stone was a legendary object he couldn't resist. What was that stone?
source_excerpt: Dumbledore recognised the symbol of the Deathly Hallows on the ring's black stone as the Resurrection Stone, which he had searched for most of his life.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember Dumbledore's withered hand as a simple curse injury. The twist is that one of Voldemort's Horcruxes secretly held a Deathly Hallow, and Dumbledore's longing to see his dead family made him slip it on.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter book lore from 2005, not tied to any current news.

extra.verification_notes: Dumbledore put on Marvolo Gaunt's Horcrux ring, whose stone was the Resurrection Stone, and the curse blackened his hand (https://www.hp-lexicon.org/magic/curse-on-the-ring).

explanation: Voldemort set one of the three Deathly Hallows into a Horcrux without realising it. Dumbledore put the ring on hoping to see his lost family again, and the curse left him with about a year to live.

question: On Harry's eleventh birthday, Hagrid takes him shopping in Diagon Alley and buys him a present at Eeylops Owl Emporium. What name does Harry give that present?
source_excerpt: Hedwig was an eleventh birthday gift from Rubeus Hagrid to Harry

extra.why_interesting: Players remember Hedwig but rarely think of her as a shop purchase. Placing the gift in Eeylops Owl Emporium turns a familiar character into a Diagon Alley shopping moment.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter book/film trivia; general culture, not tied to any news event.

extra.verification_notes: Hagrid buys Harry a snowy owl at Eeylops Owl Emporium for his 11th birthday and Harry names her Hedwig; no conflicting sources or newer developments found.

explanation: She was a snowy owl, and Harry took her name from a book on the history of magic. She was his first real friend from the wizarding world.

question: Fred and George Weasley could afford to open their Diagon Alley joke shop only because Harry handed them a bag of gold he had won. In which contest did Harry win that gold?
source_excerpt: Harry gave the twins his Triwizard Tournament winnings of 1,000 Galleons to fund their joke shop.

extra.why_interesting: Most fans know the twins' joke shop well and forget that it was paid for with Harry's tournament prize. Players have to trace the money back through the story to answer.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter plot detail; evergreen fiction trivia.

extra.verification_notes: In Goblet of Fire Harry gave his 1,000-Galleon Triwizard Tournament winnings to Fred and George, who used it to fund Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes.

explanation: Harry gave them all 1,000 Galleons because he wanted everyone to have a laugh after Cedric's death. Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes became the busiest shop on the street.

question: In the first Harry Potter film, the doorway to the Leaky Cauldron, the pub that leads into Diagon Alley, wasn't built in a studio. It was a real shopfront inside an ornate Victorian covered market in the City of London. Which market?
source_excerpt: The Glass House, 2-3 Bull's Head Passage, Leadenhall Market, EC3V 1LU.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume Diagon Alley's doorway was built in a studio. In fact you can walk up to it in a real Victorian market in London's financial district.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Filming location of a 2001 film; evergreen film/geography trivia.

extra.verification_notes: Time Out confirms the Leaky Cauldron entrance in the first film was a real shopfront (now an optician) in Bull's Head Passage, Leadenhall Market, City of London.

explanation: The doorway was an empty shop that later became an optician's, and fans still come to photograph its blue door.

question: In Hagrid's very first Care of Magical Creatures lesson, the class meets proud half-eagle, half-horse hippogriffs. What must you do before you dare step close to one?
alternative_answers: Bow and wait for it to bow back
source_excerpt: Students were told to approach slowly, bow, and hold off on touching until the animal responded.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember Buckbeak but may not recall the specific etiquette. It's easy to reconstruct from the proud, eagle-like nature of the creature, and Draco's insult that gets him slashed is the payoff.
extra.subtheme: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter book lore about hippogriff etiquette; not news.

extra.verification_notes: In Prisoner of Azkaban, Hagrid's first lesson teaches students to bow to a hippogriff and wait for it to bow back before approaching, which matches the claimed answer.

explanation: You bow, hold eye contact and wait. Only if the hippogriff bows back is it safe to approach. Draco Malfoy skipped the manners, insulted Buckbeak, and got his arm slashed for it.

question: For four years Harry thought the Hogwarts carriages pulled themselves. Then in fifth year he suddenly saw the skeletal winged horses that had been pulling them all along. What must a person have witnessed before they can see these creatures?
source_excerpt: carnivorous species of winged horse visible only to those who have experienced loss through death.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the carriages at Hogwarts are simply enchanted to move by themselves. The grim reason Harry can suddenly see the creatures pulling them reframes a cosy school ride.
extra.subtheme: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter book lore about Thestrals; general fiction trivia, not news.

extra.verification_notes: Canon (Order of the Phoenix) says only those who have seen someone die can see thestrals, and Harry saw Cedric die; Wikipedia only paraphrases this more loosely as 'loss through death'.

explanation: Thestrals are only visible to those who have seen death, and Harry had watched Cedric Diggory die at the end of the previous year. Luna could see them too, because she saw her mother die.

question: Harry Potter was a Horcrux its maker never meant to create. Who destroyed the fragment of soul hidden inside Harry?
alternative_answers: He Who Must Not Be Named
source_excerpt: the Harry Horcrux... destroyed by Voldemort's own Killing Curse in the Forbidden Forest.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the heroes destroying Horcruxes with fangs and swords, so they look for a hero. The answer is the villain himself, which feels obvious only once heard.

subtheme_plan.name: Magical creatures in Care of Magical Creatures

topicality.rationale: Harry Potter plot detail from the final book; not tied to any current event.

extra.verification_notes: Canon (Deathly Hallows) has Voldemort's own Killing Curse in the Forbidden Forest destroy the soul fragment inside Harry; no later development contradicts this (https://mugglenet.com/resources/every-horcrux-explained/).

explanation: When Voldemort hit Harry with the Killing Curse in the Forbidden Forest, he killed only his own soul fragment. Harry survived because Voldemort had taken Harry's blood, and with it Lily's protection.
